Hi Claire — great to hear from you and thanks for the PO. High level answers up front, then a proposed sketch.

1) List price vs committed discount: For AWS private offers we publish a Marketplace list price (what shows in AWS UI) and then attach the private offer which applies the committed discount. The invoice you receive from AWS will reference the Marketplace SKU and list price lines, but the private offer credit will reduce your billed amount. In practice customers see a listprice line + a negative credit line tied to the private offer.

2) Reseller margin visibility: We can accommodate a visible pass-through margin line but with two caveats: (a) AWS invoices are the primary billing instrument — if your reseller expects a separate line on invoices they typically need to be a named reseller in the AWS flow or we route a secondary settlement outside AWS (Redwood invoices/reseller invoices). Most customers prefer the latter (Redwood issues a reseller settlement invoice and credits the reseller separately).

3) Broker/dealer fees: Redwood generally does not tack an additional broker fee on top of the private offer. If there is a channel broker, we can model a dealer fee (recommended <= 4% of billable consumption) and route it as a separate Redwood settlement to the broker/reseller so AWS billing remains clean.

Proposed split for Veridian (assuming annual committed spend $1.2M):
- Marketplace list price: $1,500,000 (published SKU)
- Private-offer committed discount: 20% (applied in AWS PO -> $300k credit)
- Net billed to customer (via AWS): $1,200,000 (subject to AWS taxes/withholdings)
- Reseller uplift to show/reserve: 10% of net ($120k) — Redwood can issue a separate reseller settlement showing this margin and the supporting usage schedule.
- Dealer fee (if applicable): recommend 3-4% of net ($36k-$48k) routed as a separate Redwood pay-through.

Operational flow options (pick one):
A) AWS-only routing: Customer pays AWS; private-offer credit applied; Redwood issues reseller settlement and broker passes outside AWS. Pros: simplest for procurement. Cons: reseller needs separate invoice reconciliation.
B) Hybrid (recommended): AWS handles customer billing and private-offer credit; Redwood sends a single settlement to reseller with line-item breakdown (reseller margin + any dealer fee). This keeps AWS invoices unchanged while giving reseller the visibility they need.

Next steps: I can (1) share a revised PO PDF that mirrors the split and includes a suggested wording line for invoice routing; (2) loop in Deals Ops to lock invoice references and tax handling. Do you want me to prepare the revised PO for your review?

Soojin — thanks for the heads up. Quick answers:

1) Reseller settlement template: yes — we have a standard template that includes SKU-level usage, list price, private-offer credit, reseller margin line, and a dealer/broker fee line if needed. I'll attach the template once I refresh names/placeholders.

2) Supporting data: minimally we need per-SKU daily usage exports from AWS + AWS invoice reference numbers (invoice #, billing period). For private offers we also include the private offer ID so the credit ties back.

3) Tax & remittance: Recommended approach is to gross up dealer/broker fees and remit them on a net basis after Redwood collects the settlement. Finance prefers we treat dealer fees as a pass-through liability rather than revenue when we have explicit instructions and signed reseller agreement. Cap dealer fee at 5% — anything above requires RevOps + Legal signoff.

Jordan — if you can confirm the PO metadata fields (tax IDs, ERP codes, bill-to party), we'll include that in the revised PO wording. I can draft the external-facing PO language today.
